lines.speaker: Protesilaus
lines.text: My lord, my king, our Zeus down here—and you, daughter of Demeter—do not ignore a lover’s petition.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: And what exactly are you asking of us? Also, who are you?

lines.speaker: Protesilaus
lines.text: I am Protesilaus, son of Iphiclus, from Phylace; I sailed with the Achaeans and was the first man to die at Troy. What I ask is to be released for a little while, and come back to life.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: That particular love, Protesilaus, is shared by every dead man here. None of them gets it.

lines.speaker: Protesilaus
lines.text: But it is not life I am in love with, lord Hades. It is my wife. I left her newly married, still in the bridal chamber, when I sailed away; then, unlucky fool that I was, I died in the landing, killed by Hector. My love for her is wearing me down past bearing, my lord. I want to be seen by her, even briefly, and then come back down again.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: Did you not drink the water of Lethe, Protesilaus?

lines.speaker: Protesilaus
lines.text: I did, my lord. Plenty of it. The thing was simply too large.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: Then wait. She will arrive here herself one day, and you will not need to go up at all.

lines.speaker: Protesilaus
lines.text: I cannot bear the delay, Pluto. You have been in love yourself; you know what it is.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: And what good will one day alive do you, when a little later you will be grieving over the same thing again?

lines.speaker: Protesilaus
lines.text: I think I can persuade her to come back with me to you. So instead of one corpse, you will shortly have two.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: That is not permitted. It has never been done.

lines.speaker: Protesilaus
lines.text: Let me refresh your memory, Pluto. You handed Eurydice over to Orpheus for this very reason, and you sent my kinswoman Alcestis back with Heracles, as a favour to him.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: And you want to appear to that beautiful young bride of yours like this—a bare skull, shapeless and all? How is she even supposed to receive you, when she will not be able to recognise you? She will be frightened, I can tell you that. She will run away. Then you will have come all that way for nothing.

lines.speaker: Persephone
lines.text: Then fix that too, husband. Tell Hermes, once Protesilaus is back in the light, to touch him with the wand and make him at once into a handsome young man again—just as he was when he came out of the bridal room.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: Since Persephone agrees, take him up and make him a bridegroom again. And you—remember: you have one day.
